title: How remote brewery consultancy works | Craft Beer School
desc: What a remote consultancy engagement looks like: the health check, video calls, shared data, samples and when a site visit is worth arranging.
teaser: You do not need a consultant in your brewery every week. Most of the useful work is done through data, photos and a good call.
standfirst: Remote consultancy means working with a brewer or quality specialist by video call and shared data, with site visits by arrangement. This is how it runs in practice.
sections:
A brewery generates a lot of information every day: brew sheets, fermentation temperatures, gravity readings, pH, packaging records and cleaning logs. Most problems leave a trail in those numbers before anyone tastes anything wrong. A consultant who can read that trail does not need to be standing next to the tank.

Remote work also removes the travel cost and the delay. A fermentation that has stalled is better looked at on the day it stalls than three weeks later when someone can fly in.
Step one: the brewery health check

We start with a health check and a written action plan. You send what you already have: the process flow, a typical brew sheet, a week of fermentation records, lab results if any and photos of the plant. We read them and list what we understand, what we do not and what to look at first.

The health check ends with a short written plan: what to fix, in what order and what to measure. It is a document your team can work from without us in the room.

The plan is ranked. Items that protect beer quality or safety come first, such as cleaning routines and temperature control. Items that save money come next. Items that make the brewery nicer to run come last. The ranking matters because it stops a small team from trying to fix everything at once.

Video calls work best when they have a purpose. Typical uses are walking through a fermenter's temperature log together, watching the brewer run a CIP cycle on camera, reviewing a packaging line from the operator's phone or tasting a beer together while discussing what each of us notices.

Photos and short videos do a lot of work: a sight glass, a label, a hop addition, a burst of foam at the keg filler. We ask for them to be taken in good light and with a note of the time and the tank.

Time zones are manageable. Calls are booked at times that suit both sides and each call ends with notes sent in writing. If your brewer works an early shift, we can meet before the first brew of the day, when the plant is quiet and a camera can be pointed at whatever needs to be seen.

A shared spreadsheet is usually enough. We agree the few numbers worth tracking: original gravity, final gravity, fermentation days, brewhouse efficiency, packaging loss and any complaints. Our one-page dashboard piece shows what an owner should see on a single sheet.

Data stays with you. We ask for what is needed to solve the problem and agree who can see it before anything is shared.

Keep the numbers honest. A figure that is estimated is worse than a blank, because it leads to wrong conclusions. If a measurement is hard to take today, say so. We will suggest the cheapest way to start taking it.

Some questions cannot be answered by video. A suspected infection, an off flavour that has no obvious source or a stability problem may need a lab test. Shipping beer across borders involves rules for alcohol, so we help you think through options such as a local lab. We do not promise results from a sample we have not seen tested.
When a site visit is worth it

Remote work has limits. Commissioning a new brewhouse, a plant layout problem or a training week for a new team benefit from someone on site. Visits happen by arrangement. We say plainly when we think one is worth the cost. Our piece on commissioning with an overseas supplier covers a case where it often is.
What you should expect and what you should not

Expect clear questions, a written plan, regular calls and honest advice about what you can fix yourself. Do not expect guaranteed results. Beer depends on your equipment, your raw materials, your water and your team. Nobody can promise outcomes from a distance. The aim is to leave your team able to run the improvements without us. See also what a remote quality audit reviews and how we handle faults over video call.

A good engagement also has an end. We aim to leave your team with the habits, the sheets and the understanding to carry on. If you still want regular input after that, a short monthly call to review the numbers is a reasonable arrangement. The goal is a brewery that needs us less over time.
faqs: Can you really consult on a brewery without visiting it?
For many problems, yes. Data, photos and live video show most of what matters. Site visits are arranged when the work needs them, such as commissioning.
What do I need to send first?
A process flow, a typical brew sheet, recent fermentation and lab records and photos of the plant. Rough records are fine.
Do you work across time zones?
Yes. We schedule calls at times that suit both sides and share notes in writing.
No. We give a written plan and honest advice. Outcomes depend on your plant, ingredients and team.
